question.problem: The second-degree Taylor polynomial of $f(x)=\frac{1}{\sqrt[4]{1-x}}$ about $x=0$ is
question.worked_solution:
To find the second-degree Taylor polynomial about $x=0,$ we plug $a=0$ into the general formula to give

$$
{P}_{2}(x)=f(0)+{f}^{′}(0)(x-0)+\frac{1}{2}{f}^{″}(0)(x-0)^{2}.
$$

So, we need to work out $f(0),$ ${f}^{′}(0),$ and ${f}^{″}(0):$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x) & =\frac{1}{\sqrt[4]{1-x}}=(1-x)^{-1/4} & ⟹ &  & f(0) & =1 \\ {f}^{′}(x) & =\frac{1}{4}(1-x)^{-5/4} & ⟹ &  & {f}^{′}(0) & =\frac{1}{4} \\ {f}^{″}(x) & =\frac{5}{16}(1-x)^{-9/4} & ⟹ &  & {f}^{″}(0) & =\frac{5}{16}\end{aligned}
$$

We now plug the results for $f(0),$ ${f}^{′}(0),$ and ${f}^{″}(0)$ into our second-degree Taylor polynomial. This gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{P}_{2}(x) & =1+(\frac{1}{4})\cdot x+(\frac{5}{16})\cdot \frac{1}{2}{x}^{2} \\  & =1+\frac{1}{4}x+\frac{5}{32}{x}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$
